transcript:

Try it free for 14 days at goo.gle/workspacewithgemini.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
President Trump is planning more appearances at Republican campaign
rallies ahead of the November midterm elections.
He's scheduled to be in Georgia tomorrow and Kentucky on Saturday.
NPR's Deepa Shivaram says the president was in Montana yesterday,
outside Glacier National Park, less than three weeks before the midterms.
Montana is a red state, but Trump said he wanted to travel there to thank his supporters.
He emphasized Second Amendment rights to the crowd and callous spell
and touted his economic agenda, like tariffs, no tax on Social Security,
and his promise to give people $5,000 if Republicans keep control of Congress,
though that proposal would be costly and would likely require approval from Congress.
Trump's travel is ramping up as the latest inflation report shows bad numbers for
Republicans and the Trump administration, and polling shows Americans blame Trump for high prices.
Deepa Shivaram, NPR News.
The president is expected to attend more than 30 GOP rallies before election day.
The Justice Department is warning the state of California it may take legal action because of
non-citizens having received mail-in ballots ahead of the November midterms.
The acting deputy attorney general says the DOJ has provided the state with a list
of what's described as likely non-citizens being provided with mail-in ballots.
The DOJ is giving the state until later today to respond.
The registrar in Los Angeles County says his office is reviewing the list,
along with the state's attorney general and secretary of state.
The Vatican says Pope Leo continues to recover from surgery to remove a cancerous growth
from his right lung. NPR's Jason Derose says the pope celebrated mass yesterday.
According to the Vatican, Pope Leo has undergone routine post-op blood tests and a chest x-ray.
He's also having respiratory therapy.
Leo has been active in his first 18 months, teaching on artificial intelligence,
traveling to Africa and the Middle East, and speaking out on war and immigration.
Catholic studies professor Susan Reynolds at Emory University
says the cancer might bring something more to his papacy.
He has made a profound impact on the global church,
but in other ways it does seem like he's only just beginning.
So I imagine that this will perhaps ignite in him a certain sense of urgency.
For instance, appointing Cardinals, the people who will someday elect the next pope.
Jason Derose, NPR News.
Authorities in Pakistan say a roof collapse at a private school in the country's northwest
has left more than two dozen children dead, along with at least one teacher.
Dozens of people were injured there.
The roof gave way at the school in Peshawar.
Search and rescue efforts are continuing to try to locate those who are believed to be trapped.
Authorities say more than 100 students were in three classrooms when that roof gave way.
This is NPR News from Washington.
The tech company Global Foundry says it's planning to build two computer chip plants
in Malta, New York.
It says the Japanese government will provide $21 billion for the project.
OpenAI is being sued by eight states.
They're recusing the tech company of misleading consumers about the safety of its AI chatbot
and allege it harms children, as NPR's Shannon Bond reports.
The lawsuits filed in state courts in Arizona, Iowa, Nebraska, and five other states
accuse OpenAI of violating consumer protection laws.
They argue that while the company says chat GPT is safe,
the AI chatbot has coached users, including kids, to harm themselves or others.
The states are asking courts to force the company to change how its products work for young users
and to pay monetary damages.
They also want OpenAI barred from developing self-improving AI models,
unless it makes sure they're aligned with human values.
OpenAI says it's built "industry-leading age-specific protections"
and says it's working with states to advance industry-wide policies.
Shannon Bond, NPR News.
The Milwaukee Brewers are now one win away from an advancing to Major League Baseball's World Series.
Last night in Los Angeles, the Brewers beat the Dodgers 6-2
to take a three-games-to-none lead in the National League Championship Series.
Milwaukee hit three home runs in the win, Game 4 is tonight, again at Dodger Stadium.
The winner of the NLCS will advance to the Fall Classic
against either the Cleveland Guardians or the Tampa Bay Rays.
That series is tied at a game apiece.
I'm Dave Mattingly, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: President Trump plans more GOP rallies, including Georgia and Kentucky, after Montana appearance near Glacier National Park
Justice Department threatens legal action against California over non-citizens receiving mail-in ballots ahead of midterms
Pope Leo recovering from lung cancer surgery; Vatican reports routine post-op tests and respiratory therapy
Roof collapse at a private school in Peshawar, Pakistan kills more than two dozen children and at least one teacher
Global Foundries plans two computer chip plants in Malta, New York, with $21 billion from Japan
Eight states sue OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT misleads consumers about safety and harms children
Milwaukee Brewers beat Dodgers 6-2 to take 3-0 lead in National League Championship Series
